stories.topic: The tycoon's question: can we grow rich and still beat our wives?
stories.summary: Over dinner abroad, a friend of Amit's who runs one of Asia's biggest businesses (and holds degrees in philosophy and anthropology) posed a question. He let Amit use the question but not his name: can a society grow rich while keeping its illiberal habits, or must it give them up to prosper? Amit guessed that the median Indian male would say yes, you can grow rich and keep beating your wife. Amit's own view is that in the long run, true prosperity, even in the material sense, is impossible without modern liberal values. Ajay added two lenses. The answer may differ for an individual and for a society. And if the answer were 'no', some people might choose to give up prosperity rather than accept enlightenment values.
stories.insight: The question sets up the whole episode. It asks whether freedom is a package you must take whole, or a menu you can pick from. China bet on the menu.
stories.quote: Can we grow rich and still beat our wives? Or do we have to stop beating our wives to grow rich?

stories.topic: Samuelson's dotted line: when the USSR looked like the future
stories.summary: After 1917 the Soviets forced industrialisation through central planning and enormous cruelty. By 1945 they were the great land power, though Ajay notes they won the war with heavy Western help. They had a nuclear bomb by 1949, helped by knowledge stolen from the Manhattan Project. In edition after edition, Paul Samuelson's hugely influential economics textbook carried a GDP chart on its inside cover with a dotted projection showing the USSR overtaking the US. Orwell, Koestler and Nehru rejected the regime's cruelty, but many still thought it would 'work' in purely instrumental terms. In 1989 it collapsed under its own contradictions. Ajay says Russia has never recovered: today it has a Spain-sized GDP.
stories.insight: Even the best economists can mistake a coercive sprint for a durable growth model. The instrumental case for unfreedom failed on its own terms, not just on ethical ones.
stories.quote: Samuelson always had a dot dot dot line with projections for the future where he expected that the USSR would beat the United States in terms of its aggregate GDP.

stories.topic: Four flavours of yogurt: what China learned from the Soviet collapse
stories.summary: The Chinese Communist Party studied the fall of the USSR closely and swore to do whatever it took to survive. One lesson it drew was that consumer shortages kill regimes. So China opened up to a private consumer economy with '400 kinds of yogurt', to trade, and to FDI, while keeping one-party rule, state direction and limits on personal freedom.
stories.insight: China was not a copy of the Soviet model. It was a deliberate update: give people economic abundance and keep political control. The episode argues this update is now breaking too.
stories.quote: They understood that the Soviet Union collapsed because they were not able to make more than four kinds of flavored yogurt.

stories.topic: 'Our way is right': the 2008 meeting with Wang Qishan
stories.summary: Richard McGregor's The Party describes a 2008 meeting, just after the financial crisis hit America. A group of American businessmen met Wang Qishan, China's vice premier in charge of the financial sector. Wang told them that America has its way, China has its way, and China's way is right. Amit says the Americans could be forgiven for thinking there might be something to it.
stories.insight: The 2008 crisis gave the 'China model' its moment of confidence. Western capitalists started to doubt their own system, and global firms went all in on China.
stories.quote: you have your way. We have our way, our way is right.

stories.summary: During the Cultural Revolution, Red Guards threw Deng Xiaoping's son, then about 11 or 14 years old, out of a first-floor window. The fall broke his bones and crippled him for life. When Deng came to power in 1978, he built guardrails against a repeat of Maoism. He introduced term limits of ten years for the head of state and a succession system that neither Mao nor the Soviet Union ever had. He also set a non-confrontational 'bide our time' stance toward the West. Ajay explains that Xi Jinping later dismantled all of this.
stories.insight: Deng's reforms came from someone who had felt the regime's cruelty in his own family. This explains why he spread power out, and why Xi concentrating it again matters so much.
stories.quote: So, in a way, Deng Xiaoping deeply knew the horror of Chinese communism.

stories.summary: Amit reads from his 2016 demonetisation column. In 1958 Mao ordered every sparrow in China killed because sparrows ate farmers' grain. Countless sparrows died. But sparrows also ate locusts, and once they were gone, locusts multiplied and destroyed the crops. Famine followed, and no fewer than 45 million people died in the three years after Mao's orders. This was part of the wider Great Leap Forward.
stories.insight: This is the 'man of system' delusion in its purest form: a leader who thinks he can redesign a whole society, or an ecosystem, to fit a master plan. Amit wrote the piece to warn that we do not learn from such cautionary tales.
stories.quote: Sparrows ate locusts. And once the balance in the ecosystem changed, locusts proliferated and destroyed China's crops.

stories.summary: McGregor describes the 'red phone' sitting on the desks of the heads of a few hundred state-owned organisations. Each had its own four-digit number. When it rang, it was the party high command and you had to pick up. You could also use it to call others on the network. It became a symbol of power, corruption and decadence.
stories.insight: This is the hidden wiring of a Leninist state. Real authority runs through party channels that sit outside the formal, legal state.
stories.quote: We've heard of red tape. In China, something called the red phone was famous

stories.topic: From father's bicycle to two cars
stories.summary: In Smoke and Mirrors, her 2007-08 book on China, Pallavi Aiyar recounts a student telling her that a generation ago his father cycled many miles to work, and now he owns two cars. When Amit asked Aiyar about it on his podcast, she said this was not one student's story. Everybody told her some version of it.
stories.insight: Whatever its sins, China delivered huge generational mobility and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Amit admits India still hasn't matched this. Any honest critique of the China model has to start by acknowledging it.
stories.quote: a generation ago, my father used to ride a bicycle so many miles to work every day. I have two cars.

stories.topic: Songbirds on the expressway, and Lahore's two faces
stories.summary: Aiyar describes Beijing as surreal. Old men in Mao suits walked their caged songbirds along expressways, and elderly women practised tai chi surrounded by bulldozers. What struck her most was that people showed no visible trauma or resistance. Amit connects this to his 2006 trip to Pakistan, where he covered the Indian cricket team for The Guardian, the Wall Street Journal and Cricinfo. In Lahore, where his father was born but felt no nostalgia for, Amit found a warm, effusive Punjabi culture living alongside a darkness coming from the regime's ideology.
stories.insight: This is Amit's lament. We like to think bottom-up culture always outlasts top-down rule. But the longer an oppressive regime lasts, the more it can reshape the culture itself.
stories.quote: sometimes in this clash between an oppressive regime and a liberated culture, you know, the oppressive regime may win out.

stories.topic: Vaccine nationalism and the made-in-China milk problem
stories.summary: India made no pretence of building its own COVID vaccine. The Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine (Covishield) came to India with help from the Gates Foundation, and a private Indian company built huge manufacturing capacity with no help from the state. China, driven by nationalism and an insistence that it had 'arrived', pushed its own vaccines, which gave poor protection. Decades of coercion also meant that many older Chinese, the people most vulnerable to COVID, refused a government vaccine. Ajay notes that many Chinese won't even drink made-in-China milk.
stories.insight: Authoritarianism fails in practical terms, not just moral ones. Past coercion destroys the trust a state needs when it finally asks citizens to cooperate.
stories.quote: So if the government says this is a made in China vaccine, you know something is wrong.

stories.topic: The app that screams: China's lockdown nightmare
stories.summary: China ran some of the world's most extreme lockdowns and presented them as proof that the Chinese way was better. Month after month, people were trapped in their homes. Phones, digital identity and tracking were used so that if you stepped into the next street, an app raised an alarm and an official came after you. Production stopped, global supply chains broke, and protests broke out, which is rare in China. Eventually the regime gave up, COVID surged, and many people died.
stories.insight: Digital tools that look like conveniences in a free society can become instruments for crushing individuals in an authoritarian one.
stories.quote: people could not move into the next street because the app would start screaming, and then a government official would come after that person.

recommendations.creator: David Shambaugh
recommendations.context: Ajay's closing recommendation.
recommendations.reason: His pick if you read just one book on China. It is short and compact. Written in 2016, against the pro-China intellectuals of the time, it understood everything that would happen from 2016 to 2023. Hindsight has been very kind to it.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's first closing recommendation.
recommendations.reason: A companion to this episode. It traces India's journey from centuries before independence to today, period by period, and argues why freedom matters.

recommendations.item: The Essential Dykes To Watch Out For
recommendations.creator: Alison Bechdel
recommendations.context: Amit's second closing recommendation, taken from the pile of books on set that viewers had asked about.
recommendations.reason: The comic strip ran for roughly 1985 to 2008 and became iconic. It captured, and arguably helped create, a lesbian counterculture. Its strip 'The Rule' gave the world the Bechdel test. It is also a model of steady, week-after-week craft.

recommendations.creator: Alison Bechdel
recommendations.context: Mentioned while recommending Bechdel's comic strip.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls her 2006 memoir a masterpiece. It shows that comics can be a profound art form that competes with the best of literature.

recommendations.creator: Craig Thompson
recommendations.context: Listed alongside Fun Home as proof of what comics can do.
recommendations.reason: One of the graphic novels Amit calls a masterpiece. He says he may someday do a full list of the comics he loves.

recommendations.creator: Daniel Clowes
recommendations.context: Listed alongside Fun Home and Blankets.
recommendations.reason: Another graphic novel Amit calls a masterpiece.

recommendations.item: The Party: The Secret World of China's Communist Rulers
recommendations.creator: Richard McGregor
recommendations.context: Amit quotes it throughout his history of China.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great book on how the party really works. It shows the Leninist machinery under China's reforms: control of personnel, propaganda and the army, a party above the law, the red phone, and the 'take it or leave it' compact.

recommendations.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
recommendations.context: Her first book on China, from around 2007-08, quoted for the bicycle-to-two-cars story and the passage about Beijing's surreal cityscapes.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Aiyar a fantastic writer and a sharp analyst, not just a travel writer. The book gives a ground-level view of China's transformation and how people absorbed it.

recommendations.item: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
recommendations.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
recommendations.context: Amit reads its parable of the pauper and two finance gurus to set up a question on how poor countries escape poverty.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a really interesting book. Its framing of the poverty trap provokes debate, and Amit says he even has a problem with the framing itself.

recommendations.creator: Timur Kuran
recommendations.context: Cited to explain how the Soviet Union suddenly unravelled.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a fantastic book. It explains preference falsification and preference cascades: regimes look unanimously supported until people discover that others secretly disagree too.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (Episode 349 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Timur Kuran
recommendations.context: Show-notes link accompanying the discussion of preference cascades.
recommendations.reason: Amit's longer conversation with Kuran himself, for anyone who wants to go deeper into the ideas behind the Soviet collapse.

recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Mentioned as 'that famous essay' written as the Soviet Union fell.
recommendations.reason: It captured the post-1989 sense that liberal democracy had won the argument. The China model later revived that very debate.

recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Amit reads the full 'man of system' passage from it.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great book that is often overlooked. It coined the 'man of system', the planner who treats people like chess pieces, which is the best warning against Maoist-style grand designs.

recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Cited right after Smith's 'man of system' passage.
recommendations.reason: Amit says Hayek's phrase 'the fatal conceit' aptly expresses the same idea: the belief that planners can design a society.

recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Amit tells how Margaret Thatcher slammed it on the table at her first cabinet meeting and said it would guide them.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Thatcher one of his heroes of the 20th century and Hayek his favourite 'Freddie'. It is the classic argument for freedom against state planning.

recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Show-notes link, listed with Hayek's other books.
recommendations.reason: Rounds out the Hayek reading behind the episode's case for freedom.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Asked what he would do in Deng's place, Ajay recalls the question behind the book: if a time machine could carry one book to Nehru, which should it be?
recommendations.reason: Ajay says it would have been a very good book for Deng Xiaoping as well, because its message is to fix the freedom side first. Amit calls it 'the greatest plug I've ever seen somebody give for their own freaking book.'

recommendations.item: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His 2016 demonetisation piece, from which he reads the sparrow-campaign passage. He says it went madly viral.
recommendations.reason: It links Mao's grand designs to demonetisation through one shared delusion: that a leader can redesign society to fit a master plan.

recommendations.item: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Amit asks whether China's GDP growth was hollow.
recommendations.reason: It covers his long-standing problem with GDP. Because government spending counts in GDP, a state can inflate the number with make-work and roads to nowhere.

recommendations.item: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link accompanying Ajay's comparison of India's and China's vaccine approaches.
recommendations.reason: The longer conversation on vaccine economics and politics behind Ajay's COVID argument.

recommendations.item: India's Greatest Civil Servant (Episode 167 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Narayani Basu
recommendations.context: Linked to Amit's discussion of how Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon put the Indian Union together after independence.
recommendations.reason: Amit uses that history as his own unresolved case of ends and means. He calls it 'fast-track colonization', achieved through coercion and broken promises.

recommendations.item: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Episode 11 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit uses the phrase to describe how Bechdel produced her strip week after week for decades.
recommendations.reason: Explains the mantra behind his praise of Bechdel: keep doing the work, again and again.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's thesis is that economic, political and personal freedoms rise and fall together, and real prosperity needs all of them. The Soviet Union bet that it needed none. China bet that limited economic freedom alone was enough. Ajay adds two lenses. The answer may differ for an individual and a society. And if freedom really is indivisible, some people may choose to give up prosperity rather than accept enlightenment values.
core_ideas.quote: if we are to prosper as people, to grow as individuals, all kinds of freedom have to come hand in hand.

core_ideas.explanation: Coercive regimes can mobilise resources and sprint for a while. But they pile up distortions, much like technical debt in software, and eventually the bill comes due. The old argument goes: 'be thuggish first, get rich, then add democracy'. Some made it about India in 1947, when female literacy was only 6-7%. Ajay's answer is that a society built on coercion cannot easily switch into freedom. Chile, Taiwan and South Korea managed the transition, but it is hard.
core_ideas.quote: you can run up a lot of debt and you can appear to make some progress, but your sins are going to catch up with you. And then the whole thing falls apart.

core_ideas.concept: Coordination by coercion looks like success
core_ideas.explanation: Free markets coordinate messily through prices and private bargains, and nobody can tell where they will lead. A state can force everyone onto one standard, as China did with a single payment system, much like UPI. That produces fast, visible wins. Such short-term wins are why so many admirers took China as proof that industrial policy and wise officials could guide an economy.
core_ideas.quote: A state-led industrial policy can, however, align everybody in the country around one project, one standard.

core_ideas.explanation: In every free country there are thinkers who want less freedom. Some are social conservatives who see free people as degenerate. Some are would-be rulers hungry for power without checks and balances. Some are fans of industrial policy. They admired the USSR, then turned to China. Global business followed along, partly because, as Ajay says, practitioners inside firms tend to follow the prevailing consensus.
core_ideas.quote: In every free country, there has been a camp of thinkers who have argued in favor of less freedom.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay frames the whole story as a history of ideas. The Soviet Union's achievements and horrors both came from one scholar's thinking. So the most important debate is over which ideas societies adopt, and freedom is the central one.
core_ideas.quote: So in the end, it is all about ideas. Nothing matters more than ideas.

core_ideas.explanation: This is Timur Kuran's framework. Under repression, everyone hides what they really think, so the regime looks universally supported. Once people realise others share their discontent, the silence turns into a cascade and the regime collapses suddenly. Amit uses this to explain the fall of the USSR.
core_ideas.quote: while the Soviet Union was active, it never seemed like anybody was against it, because every individual was scared to speak up

core_ideas.explanation: Adam Smith's warning: the planner falls in love with his own ideal plan and imagines he can move people around like chess pieces. Hayek called the same error 'the fatal conceit'. Mao's sparrow campaign and demonetisation are Amit's examples. Each person has their own reasons for acting, and plans that ignore this end in disaster.
core_ideas.quote: in the great chessboard of human society, every single piece has a principle of motion of its own, altogether different from that which the legislature might choose to impress upon it.

core_ideas.explanation: Even after Deng's reforms, McGregor and the historian Robert Service both find China still recognisably communist. The party controls personnel, propaganda and the army, along with the cadres and the news. It sits above the law and is not even registered as an organisation that could be sued.
core_ideas.quote: Peek under the hood of the Chinese model, however, and China looks much more communist than it does on the open road.

core_ideas.explanation: McGregor's description of the post-Mao bargain: stay out of politics, and you and your family can get on with life and maybe get rich. Propaganda backs it up by telling people that only the party stands between China and chaos. Read the other way, the compact says 'get rich or else'. It holds only while growth delivers.
core_ideas.quote: If you play by the party's rules, which means eschewing competitive politics, then you and your family can get on with your lives and maybe get rich.

core_ideas.explanation: In a free economy, business cycles are normal. Policy can soften them, but no one can 'manage' an economy. China pulled four levers year after year to hit GDP targets: land rules, construction, infrastructure and credit. On paper it seemed to have beaten the business cycle. In reality the credit turned into bad loans within two or three years. As the economy grew, the levers became too weak for problems worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
core_ideas.quote: So whenever there's a GDP target, you gotta get nervous that something is not going right in this country.

core_ideas.concept: Roads to nowhere: GDP versus return on equity
core_ideas.explanation: Government spending counts in GDP. So a state can boost the headline number with make-work, roads to nowhere and empty cities. Amit calls such growth 'a shadow, a chimera'. Ajay's test is return on equity. A private developer won't build a road to nowhere because they worry about getting paid. The state will.
core_ideas.quote: A good infrastructure project is one that earns some plausible return on equity.

core_ideas.explanation: Marx was right that capitalism swings between booms and busts, and wrong that the swings would keep worsening. Ajay argues the busts are necessary because they create the right incentives. China's endless pump-priming produced a generation of 50-year-old business leaders who had never seen a downturn and didn't understand risk. Capital went to whoever borrowed most and got closest to the party.
core_ideas.quote: I will go so far as to argue that it works through boom and bust. It needs booms and busts to create the correct incentives.

core_ideas.concept: The four elites and the populist playbook
core_ideas.explanation: Every society has four elites: the state (officials and politicians), business, intellectuals and culture. Populists capture the state and turn it on the other three, often under the banner of anti-corruption. Under Xi, the threatened families responded by sending their children and money abroad, and that loss of confidence hit the economy hard.
core_ideas.quote: In every society, there are four elites: there is the state, which is the officials and the politicians, there is the business elite, there is the intellectual elite, and there is the cultural elite.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's point is that the distrust is practical, not moral. Authoritarian rulers face no pressure to perform, so they tend to be incompetent. Ajay adds that every act of state cruelty teaches the victim's hundred friends and family that the regime cannot be trusted. That built-up distrust came due during COVID.
core_ideas.quote: When you've lived in an authoritarian country, you know the government is an enemy and not a friend.

core_ideas.concept: Authoritarianism breeds a culture of obedience
core_ideas.explanation: Decades of authoritarian rule kill initiative, creativity and the willingness to be a maverick. People learn to look up and wait for orders. Culture lives in instinct, and so do the habits of freedom. That is why a country cannot flip from communism to liberal democracy overnight: the institutions and the know-how of being free can't be switched on at will.
core_ideas.quote: Culture is what we do when we don't know what we are doing.

core_ideas.concept: India's rent-seeking streak is institutional, not cultural
core_ideas.explanation: Amit offers this as an open-source idea he once planned to write up with a friend. The habit of making money by exploiting others or colluding with the state is not part of Indian or Hindu culture. It grew out of the all-powerful state built from the 1940s to the 1970s, which suppressed private enterprise. Under it, the best way to make money was to work for the state or collude with it in zero-sum games.
core_ideas.quote: this particular facet is not something part of Indian culture or Hindu culture or anything like that. It has come out of the institutions that we built in the 40s and 50s and 60s and 70s

core_ideas.concept: Ends, means, and the limits of money
core_ideas.explanation: Asked whether China's prosperity justified its methods, Ajay answers on two levels. Ethically, state murder and cruelty are beyond the pale, and income gains add less to happiness than people assume. Instrumentally, coercive growth stalls badly. A stuck China with many young men and few prospects is fertile ground for nationalism and military aggression, including against India.
core_ideas.quote: the thrill that you and I got as a child when we got our first bicycle is not that different from the thrill when we got our first car.

core_ideas.concept: The elite as a bridge to globalisation
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay is an optimist. Following Adam Smith, he sees growth as the natural state of affairs wherever there is a tolerable level of justice, and state oppression as what holds it back. A poor country with a capable elite can plug into the world economy through export-led growth and FDI once it has freedom. A country with equally low human capital everywhere must first build that small capable pool, which takes much longer. Either way, full transformation takes generations, not 50 years.
core_ideas.quote: as long as there is a certain level of elite capability, it can be the bridge and connect into globalization. And then you're off to the races.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's verdict: Deng kept a high-modernist class of bureaucrats and technocrats steering the country, and that was the core flaw. The lesson is to fix freedom first. Amit pushes back: if Deng's goal was simply to lift hundreds of millions out of poverty within tight constraints, he succeeded. Ajay replies that great statesmen play for 50 to 100 years. Measured that way, Taiwan, not China, is the success story.
core_ideas.quote: You need to really fix the freedom side first. You need to get on the journey to a lot more freedom. Then good things will come.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay names five forces breaking the China model. First, a return to Maoist and Leninist politics: term limits scrapped, power concentrated, grievance-driven nationalism. Second, COVID mismanagement. Third, confrontation with the advanced economies, which make up 60-70% of world GDP, plus debt diplomacy with countries like Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Fourth, unsustainable economic management. Fifth, the populist attack on the other elites. The regime and the borders are intact. But like the USSR in 1989, the model has lost credibility, and global firms see they bet too much on it.
core_ideas.quote: this whole package of grievance and anger and nationalism is really toxic and the China model is broken and it will not work.

core_ideas.explanation: Ayush Patnaik asked Ajay a question. Take an Indian woman at any percentile of income and move her to the same percentile in China, where she would also earn more. Would she prefer China? Patnaik's view is yes everywhere except the elite, because Chinese society is fundamentally better for women. Amit coins a name for how much income an Indian woman would give up just to have China's greater social freedoms.
core_ideas.quote: Chinese society is fundamentally better for women than is the case with India. So this is a very bracing thing for us in India to think about.

core_ideas.explanation: This comes from Alison Bechdel's strip 'The Rule'. It is a simple frame that exposes how male-centred cinema, and history itself, have been. Amit guesses almost every Bollywood film fails it.
core_ideas.quote: Criteria one, the film has to have at least two women in it. Criteria two, those two women have to be talking to each other. Criteria three, they have to be talking to each other about something other than a man.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on post-Soviet Russia: 'It's a Spain sized GDP. Frankly, it's just Saudi Arabia with nukes.' Amit imagines listeners from Spain and Saudi Arabia protesting in Hindi: why drag us into this?

While Ajay is explaining roads to nowhere, Amit: 'we are private capitalists and Everything is Everything is like a road to nowhere. Where are the returns? We are just spending on it. It's a labor of love, no returns.' Ajay: 'we are socialists in our personal life.'
After Ajay compares the thrill of a first bicycle with a first car, Amit: 'Can I make a shameful confession? I love my car, but I don't know how to ride a cycle.'
Ajay suggests his own book, In Service of the Republic, for Deng Xiaoping. Amit: 'That is the greatest plug I've ever seen somebody give for their own freaking book.'
On Shambaugh's China's Future, Amit: 'I hadn't heard of this book till 30 seconds ago, boss. If you had told me, I would have read it and taken notes and seemed more knowledgeable than I am.'
Amit: 'you're a card-carrying economist as you have described yourself. I've never seen your card.'
Amit calls Hayek 'one of our favorite Freddies'. After the Thatcher story he adds: 'So she had the same favorite Freddie as I do.'
As Ajay describes Xi stoking grievance, nationalism and hatred of elites, Amit says drily: 'I was thinking all of this sounds familiar, but carry on.'
Ajay declares that 'the blushes of the China model rose'. Amit: 'What a line. I would urge my writing students to not learn from this and do things like this.'
How World War II was won, attributed by Ajay to either Churchill or Stalin: the Americans gave the treasure, the Russians gave the blood, and the British gave the time.
Ajay calls Karl Marx 'an academic scribbler' who 'never saw the outside of the world other than sitting inside the British Library', and says his ideas still shaped the whole Soviet experiment.
Deng Xiaoping's foreign-policy maxim, 'bide our time'. Xi Jinping abandoned it.
The party's verdict on Mao, as Amit recalls it from a 1981 party conference: Mao was 70% right and 30% wrong, with his merits primary and his errors secondary.
A Chinese professor quoted by McGregor: 'the party is like God. He is everywhere. You just can't see him.' Law professor He Weifang adds that the party 'is not even registered as an organization'.
A Chinese leader's three principles for political reform, quoted by McGregor: the party controls the armed forces, the party controls cadres, and the party controls the news.

Before the 2007 Party Congress, Edict 19 of the propaganda department told editors to strictly control coverage of the October Revolution anniversary and 'not play up the disintegration of the Soviet Union'.

A Chinese state office named 'Measures for Internment and Deportation of Urban Vagrants and Beggars'. Amit says it is self-explanatory. Shanghai lawyer Zheng Enchong lists what people faced: surveillance, home searches, detention, re-education through labour, and being locked in psychiatric asylums.
Margaret Thatcher at her first cabinet meeting, slamming Hayek's The Road to Serfdom on the table: 'Gentlemen. This is what will guide us.'
Amit on how authoritarian regimes reshape culture over time: 'as they say paradigms change one funeral at a time.'
